title: Resulting trusts
subtitle: Automatic and presumed resulting trusts, and the presumption of advancement
objectives: Distinguish automatic and presumed resulting trusts, and identify which doctrinal question each one answers

State the presumption of advancement, identify the relationships it applies to, and correctly state its current legal status — including the fact that s 199 Equality Act 2010 has never been brought into force

Apply the resulting trust framework to purchase-in-another's-name fact patterns, and distinguish commercial or investment purchases (Laskar) from family-home disputes now governed by the common intention constructive trust

leadingAuthorities.role: Automatic resulting trust arising where a trust fails to dispose of the whole beneficial interest

leadingAuthorities.citation: Westdeutsche Landesbank v Islington LBC [1996] AC 669
leadingAuthorities.role: House of Lords' account of the theoretical basis for resulting trusts; rejects a free-standing unjust enrichment basis
House of Lords casts doubt on the presumption of advancement's fit with modern domestic life
Confirms the resulting trust (rather than common intention constructive trust) analysis for a purchase made for investment purposes
Would abolish the presumption of advancement — enacted but never commenced; the presumption remains live law

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Resulting trusts sit underneath half the property-and-trusts problem questions you'll see, usually disguised as 'who paid for what'. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this brief note appears: 'You can define both categories — this lesson is about spotting which one a fact pattern is actually testing.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You already know the automatic/presumed distinction cold. The test pool below leans heavily on fact patterns — expect purchase-price scenarios, not definitions.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Slow down through Parts 1 to 3. The rest of this lesson assumes you can state, without prompting, what triggers a presumed resulting trust and when the presumption of advancement displaces it.

overview.hook: A father buys a flat and puts it in his son's name. A woman buys a flat and puts it in her husband's name. On facts that look identical, equity starts from opposite presumptions about what each of them meant to do — and one of those presumptions rests on a piece of legislation that has been sitting on the statute book, switched off, for over fifteen years.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 1 September 2026. Flagged for currency: s 199 Equality Act 2010, which would abolish the presumption of advancement, received Royal Assent in 2010 but has never been brought into force by commencement order. No date for commencement has been announced. The presumption of advancement therefore remains live, operative law today, notwithstanding that many summaries — and some out-of-date study materials — describe it as abolished. This lesson states the law as it actually stands, not as s 199 would make it if commenced.

parts.heading: Two trusts, one name, different jobs
parts.voice: structural — sets out the taxonomy before either category is explored
body: 'Resulting trust' is a single label doing two quite different jobs, and conflating them is the single most common error in this area. Both describe beneficial ownership 'jumping back' (from the Latin resultare, to spring back) to someone who transferred or paid for property — but they arise for entirely different reasons.

An automatic resulting trust arises where an express trust fails to dispose of the whole beneficial interest — a settlor carves out trusts that don't exhaust the property, or a trust fails for some other reason, and equity will not tolerate a beneficial vacuum. The surplus results back to the settlor automatically, as a matter of property law filling a gap, not because anyone's intention is being inferred or presumed.

A presumed resulting trust is a different animal entirely. It arises where someone transfers property to another gratuitously, or pays towards a purchase put into another's name, and there is no evidence either way of what they intended. Equity fills that evidential gap with a rebuttable presumption: absent more, you didn't intend a gift. Keep these two apart as you read on — the second is where nearly all the doctrinal difficulty, and all of today's live-law flag, actually sits.

components.definition: A trust under which the beneficial interest in property returns ('results') to the person who transferred it or provided the purchase money — arising either automatically, to fill a gap left by a failed or incomplete express trust, or by a rebuttable presumption where a transfer or purchase is otherwise unexplained.

interaction.prompt: Name the two recognised categories of resulting trust.
acceptableAnswers: automatic resulting trust and presumed resulting trust
interaction.modelAnswer: Automatic resulting trusts, which fill a gap left when an express trust fails to dispose of the whole beneficial interest, and presumed resulting trusts, which arise from a rebuttable presumption on an unexplained gratuitous transfer or purchase in another's name.

parts.heading: Presumed resulting trusts: the purchase-price and voluntary-transfer cases
parts.voice: case-narrative — builds the doctrine through the two fact patterns it actually governs
body: The presumed resulting trust arises in two recurring fact patterns. First, the purchase price resulting trust: A provides some or all of the purchase money for property, but legal title is put into B's name (or into A and B jointly). Equity presumes A did not intend to make B a gift of that contribution — B holds the property, or a proportionate share of it, on trust for A. Second, the voluntary transfer case: A simply transfers property they already own into B's name for no consideration. The same presumption applies.

Neither presumption is hard to rebut. It yields to any evidence of the transferor's actual intention — a stated gift, a loan agreement, evidence of a wholly different arrangement. The presumption exists only to allocate the burden of proof where the facts are otherwise silent; it is a starting point, not a conclusion.

This is also where the presumption of advancement — the subject of Part 3 — earns its keep: in certain relationships, equity presumes the opposite. Before you can spot when that counter-presumption applies, you need the baseline firmly fixed: contribution or gratuitous transfer, without more, presumptively creates a trust back to the person who paid or gave.

components.label: When a presumed resulting trust arises
points: A pays some or all of the purchase price, but title is taken in B's name — presumption of a trust for A in proportion to contribution
A voluntarily transfers property they already own into B's name for no consideration — same presumption
The presumption is rebuttable by any evidence of A's actual intention (gift, loan, or other arrangement)
It does not apply to the family home between cohabiting or married couples, where the common intention constructive trust framework (Stack v Dowden; Jones v Kernott) now governs instead

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact that triggers a presumed resulting trust analysis in this scenario.
interaction.scenarioText: Amara and her business partner Ben are buying a warehouse as a joint investment. Amara pays the full deposit from her own savings; the property is registered in Ben's sole name because only Ben qualifies for the mortgage product on offer.
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. It's the mismatch between who paid (Amara) and who holds legal title (Ben) that opens the presumed resulting trust door — the presumption then operates in Amara's favour absent contrary evidence.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the mismatch between the money and the title. Amara paying the deposit isn't itself the trigger — it only matters because title ends up somewhere other than her name.

parts.heading: The presumption of advancement — and the statute that never woke up
parts.voice: critical — states the doctrine plainly, then interrogates its currency and its politics
body: In certain relationships, equity presumes the opposite of a resulting trust: it presumes a gift. This is the presumption of advancement, and it applies where the transferor stands in a relationship of moral obligation to provide for the transferee — historically: husband to wife, father to child, and anyone standing in loco parentis to a child. A father who buys a flat in his son's name is presumed to have intended a gift; a son who buys a flat in his father's name is not — the presumption simply does not run in reverse.

The doctrine has always attracted criticism for its dated assumptions: it applies husband-to-wife but not wife-to-husband, father-to-child but not (at common law) mother-to-child. Judicial unease with this asymmetry is long-standing — Lord Diplock's leading speech in Pettitt v Pettitt questioned whether presumptions built on Victorian domestic arrangements had any real purchase on modern marriage, foreshadowing the shift of most family-home disputes onto the common intention constructive trust instead.

Parliament responded — eventually. Section 199 of the Equality Act 2010 would abolish the presumption of advancement outright. Here is the point this lesson exists to flag clearly: s 199 received Royal Assent in 2010, but it has never been commenced. No commencement order has ever been made, and none is currently scheduled. The presumption of advancement is not abolished. It remains live, operative law today, in exactly its old-fashioned form — a fact routinely misstated by students (and some out-of-date materials) who assume the Equality Act simply took care of it.

components.text: The presumption of advancement (by which, for example, a husband is presumed to be making a gift to his wife if he transfers property to her, or purchases property in her name) is abolished.
elements: Enacted by Parliament in 2010 (s 199, with s 216 requiring a commencement order)
No commencement order has ever been made
The section is therefore not in force
The presumption of advancement continues to apply as pre-2010 case law states it

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often state that 'the presumption of advancement was abolished by the Equality Act 2010' as settled law.
components.whyItsWrong: Section 199 was enacted but s 216(3) makes it commence only on a day appointed by order — and no such order has ever been made. The presumption is dormant legislation, not current law. Until commenced, the presumption of advancement continues to operate exactly as the pre-2010 authorities describe it.

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that s 199 Equality Act 2010 is currently in force, abolishing the presumption of advancement?
sliderLabels: Never brought into force — presumption still applies
interaction.explanation: Section 199 has never been commenced. The presumption of advancement remains live law today — this is one of the most commonly misstated points in this entire topic.

parts.heading: What is a resulting trust actually responding to? The Westdeutsche fight
parts.voice: argumentative — states the academic challenge before giving the House of Lords' answer, and treats the disagreement as live
body: Why does equity impose a resulting trust at all? For decades this looked like a settled, almost mechanical question of evidence and presumption. Then restitution scholars — most influentially Robert Chambers — argued for a unifying theory: resulting trusts, on this view, respond to the recipient's unjust enrichment at the transferor's expense, whenever the recipient's intention to receive the property beneficially is absent. On this account, automatic and presumed resulting trusts aren't really two different things; they're both instances of one underlying principle about absence of intention to benefit the recipient.

The House of Lords confronted this directly in Westdeutsche Landesbank v Islington LBC, in the context of a bank seeking a resulting trust over money paid under a void interest-rate swap. Lord Browne-Wilkinson rejected the unjust enrichment account as the basis for resulting trusts in English law. On his analysis, both categories still turn on intention, not absence of enrichment: a presumed resulting trust responds to the transferor's presumed intention not to benefit the recipient, while an automatic resulting trust arises because the settlor never disposed of that part of the beneficial interest in the first place — it is a default rule of property law filling an ownership gap, not a restitutionary response to the recipient's state of mind or enrichment.

This is contested ground, and it is worth teaching as contested: Westdeutsche is the law, but the academic critique it rejected has never gone away, and examiners who want to test genuine understanding (rather than recall) will often ask you to explain why the House of Lords rejected the unjust enrichment analysis, not just to state that it did.

components.caseName: Westdeutsche Landesbank Girozentrale v Islington LBC
components.factsShort: A bank paid money to a local authority under an interest-rate swap later held void as ultra vires. The bank sought a resulting trust over the payments to claim compound interest.
components.ratioShort: There is no resulting trust over money paid under a contract believed valid at the time of payment; more generally, resulting trusts respond to the transferor's actual or presumed intention, not to the recipient's unjust enrichment.

expanded.facts: Islington LBC received payments from Westdeutsche under an interest-rate swap agreement that was later declared void because local authorities had no power to enter such transactions. Westdeutsche sought restitution and, crucially, argued that a resulting trust arose over the payments from the moment of receipt, which would have let it claim compound rather than simple interest.
expanded.judgmentExtract: Lord Browne-Wilkinson held that no trust arose: the council's conscience was not affected at the time of receipt, since both parties believed the contract valid. He went further to set out a general statement of resulting trust principle, holding that a presumed resulting trust turns on the presumed intention of the transferor, and that an automatic resulting trust arises simply because the settlor has not disposed of the whole beneficial interest — not because equity is responding to any unjust enrichment of the recipient.
expanded.significance: Westdeutsche is the leading modern authority on the theoretical basis of the resulting trust in English law, and it is the House of Lords' clearest rejection of the restitutionary (unjust enrichment) account of the doctrine associated with academic writers such as Robert Chambers. The disagreement between the courts' intention-based analysis and the academic unjust-enrichment analysis remains a live debate in the literature, even though Westdeutsche states the current law.

interaction.prompt: According to Lord Browne-Wilkinson in Westdeutsche, what is the correct basis for an automatic resulting trust?
options: The recipient has been unjustly enriched at the transferor's expense
The settlor has failed to dispose of the whole beneficial interest, so equity fills the gap as a matter of property law
The recipient's conscience is affected because they knew the transfer was defective
interaction.trapExplanation: The unjust enrichment answer is the academic (Chambers) account that Westdeutsche itself rejects as the basis for English resulting trust doctrine — a tempting answer precisely because it's the theory students often meet first, but it is not what the House of Lords held.

parts.heading: Where the resulting trust still does real work today
parts.voice: comparative — sets two contexts side by side to show where the doctrine survives and where it's been displaced
body: By the early 2000s, the purchase price resulting trust had been largely pushed out of one context where it used to dominate: disputes between cohabiting or married couples over the family home. Pettitt v Pettitt itself was an early sign of judicial discomfort with mechanically applying resulting trust presumptions to domestic life, and the House of Lords later replaced that analysis for the family home with the common intention constructive trust (Stack v Dowden; Jones v Kernott) — a framework built around the parties' whole course of dealing, not a snapshot of who paid what at the point of purchase.

But 'displaced in the family home' does not mean 'abolished'. Laskar v Laskar is the case to hold onto here: a mother and daughter bought a former council house together, not to live in as a shared home, but as a commercial investment to be let out. The Court of Appeal held that the resulting trust — not the common intention constructive trust — was the right framework, precisely because the purchase was made for investment rather than domestic purposes. Purnell LJ's reasoning turned on the character of the transaction, not on the fact that the parties happened to be related.

The exam-ready version of this: ask what the property was bought for. A shared home between a couple points to Stack/Jones and the common intention constructive trust. A joint purchase for investment, business, or letting — even between family members, even between friends — points back to the older resulting trust analysis of Part 2. Getting this framing choice right is usually worth more marks than anything that follows from it.

components.title: Which framework applies: resulting trust or common intention constructive trust?
components.description: A decision path for choosing between the purchase price resulting trust and the common intention constructive trust on a joint-purchase fact pattern.

nodes.label: Property purchased or transferred with a mismatch between who paid and who holds title
Purchased as a shared home between cohabitants or spouses?
Yes → common intention constructive trust (Stack v Dowden; Jones v Kernott) — whole course of dealing
No → purchased for investment, business, or letting purposes (even between relatives)?
Yes → presumed resulting trust analysis applies (Laskar v Laskar)

components.textAlternative: Start from a mismatch between who paid and who holds title. If the property was purchased as a shared home between cohabitants or spouses, apply the common intention constructive trust framework from Stack v Dowden and Jones v Kernott, looking at the whole course of dealing. If instead the property was purchased for investment, business, or letting purposes — even between relatives, as in Laskar v Laskar — the presumed resulting trust analysis still applies.

interaction.prompt: Which scenario should be analysed using the presumed resulting trust framework, rather than the common intention constructive trust?
interaction.scenarioA: Two romantic partners buy a house together to live in as their family home; one contributes more of the deposit than the other.
interaction.scenarioB: A mother and her adult daughter jointly buy a flat purely to let out to tenants for rental income, never intending to live there themselves.
interaction.explanation: B mirrors Laskar v Laskar: an investment purchase, not a shared home, so the older resulting trust analysis (tracking contributions to the purchase price) applies even though the buyers are family. A is a shared-home purchase between a couple, which falls under the common intention constructive trust framework instead.

testPool.prompt: What is the effect of a rebuttable presumption in the context of a presumed resulting trust?
acceptableAnswers: it allocates the burden of proof absent evidence of actual intention
it presumes no gift was intended unless rebutted by evidence
testPool.modelAnswer: It sets the starting point where the transferor's intention is otherwise unexplained: equity presumes no gift was intended, so the recipient holds on trust — but that presumption yields to any evidence of the transferor's actual intention.

testPool.prompt: Does the presumption of advancement presume a gift, or a trust?
options: A gift
A trust

testPool.prompt: Which of the following relationships attracts the presumption of advancement at common law?
options: Wife transferring property to husband
Father transferring property to child
Mother transferring property to child
testPool.trapExplanation: The presumption is notoriously one-directional and dated: it runs husband-to-wife and father-to-child (and person in loco parentis to child), but not wife-to-husband or, at common law, mother-to-child — exactly the asymmetry Pettitt v Pettitt criticised.

testPool.prompt: Has s 199 Equality Act 2010, which would abolish the presumption of advancement, ever been brought into force?
options: No — it has never been commenced
Yes — it came into force alongside the rest of the Act in 2010

testPool.prompt: Section 216(3) Equality Act 2010 provides that s 199 comes into force 'on such day as the Secretary of State may by order appoint'. Given no such order has ever been made, what is the current status of the presumption of advancement?
options: It continues to apply exactly as the pre-2010 case law states it
It applies only in cases decided after 2010
It has been informally abolished by judicial practice even though the section is dormant

testPool.prompt: In the passage below adapted from Westdeutsche Landesbank v Islington LBC, highlight the sentence that states the basis of an automatic resulting trust.
testPool.passage: The claimant argued that a resulting trust responds to the unjust enrichment of the recipient. Lord Browne-Wilkinson rejected that analysis. Where a settlor fails to dispose of the whole beneficial interest under an express trust, the undisposed-of interest remains with, or results back to, the settlor as a matter of the property not having left him — this is a default rule filling a gap in title, not a response to the recipient's enrichment.
testPool.ratioSentence: Where a settlor fails to dispose of the whole beneficial interest under an express trust, the undisposed-of interest remains with, or results back to, the settlor as a matter of the property not having left him — this is a default rule filling a gap in title, not a response to the recipient's enrichment.

testPool.prompt: Order the steps of a presumed resulting trust analysis on a purchase-in-another's-name fact pattern.
items: Identify who contributed to the purchase price and who holds legal title
Ask whether a relationship attracting the presumption of advancement exists between them
If it does, presume a gift; if not, presume a resulting trust for the contributor
Consider any evidence of actual intention that would rebut whichever presumption applies

testPool.prompt: Which scenario is governed by the purchase price resulting trust rather than the common intention constructive trust?
testPool.scenarioA: Two friends jointly buy a residential buy-to-let flat purely as a rental investment, with no intention of either living there.
testPool.scenarioB: A married couple buy a house together as their matrimonial home, with one spouse contributing more of the deposit.
testPool.explanation: A tracks Laskar v Laskar: an investment purchase between co-buyers who never intend to occupy it, so the resulting trust framework governs. B is a shared family home between spouses, which falls under Stack v Dowden and Jones v Kernott instead.

testPool.prompt: A father, with no discussion of the reason, transfers a buy-to-let flat he owns outright into his adult son's sole name for no payment. On these facts alone, what is the presumed position?
options: A gift to the son, under the presumption of advancement
A resulting trust for the father, since father and child do not attract the presumption of advancement
No presumption arises because there was no purchase, only a transfer
testPool.explanation: Father-to-child gratuitous transfers attract the presumption of advancement, presuming a gift rather than a resulting trust. This is rebuttable, but on the bare facts given, the presumed position is a gift.

testPool.prompt: A woman transfers her flat into her husband's sole name for no consideration, with nothing said about why. On these facts alone, what is the presumed position?
options: A resulting trust for the wife, since the presumption of advancement does not run wife-to-husband
A gift to the husband, under the presumption of advancement
The presumption cannot apply because they are married
testPool.explanation: The presumption of advancement historically runs husband-to-wife, not wife-to-husband. Absent that presumption, the ordinary presumed resulting trust applies: a gratuitous transfer is presumed not to be a gift, so the husband is presumed to hold on trust for the wife.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that determines which presumption applies in this scenario.
testPool.scenarioText: Priya pays the whole purchase price for a cottage. She has it registered in the name of her adult nephew, whom she has never treated as her own child and does not financially support.
tappableSpans: registered in the name of her adult nephew
never treated as her own child
testPool.correctSpan: never treated as her own child
testPool.explanation: The presumption of advancement extends to a person standing in loco parentis to the transferee, not simply to any relative. Because Priya has never stood in that relationship to her nephew, the ordinary presumed resulting trust applies in her favour rather than the presumption of advancement.

testPool.prompt: Deniz pays 70% of the purchase price of a flat bought jointly with his adult daughter Elif, who pays the remaining 30% and takes out the mortgage in her sole name because only she qualifies for the lending. They intend to let the flat out as an investment and never to live in it. Deniz later claims a resulting trust reflecting his 70% contribution. Elif argues the presumption of advancement means the whole flat is a gift to her. Analyse Deniz's claim.
factsToOrder: Deniz pays 70% of the purchase price
Legal title and the mortgage are in Elif's sole name
The purchase is for investment/letting, not as a shared home
No express discussion of the parties' intentions took place

Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether Deniz can claim a resulting trust in Elif's favour reflecting his 70% contribution, or whether the presumption of advancement defeats that claim.
modelAnswer.rule: A purchase price resulting trust is presumed where a contributor's payment is not reflected in legal title, unless the presumption of advancement applies (as it can between father and child) and is not rebutted; investment purchases are analysed under the resulting trust framework rather than the common intention constructive trust (Laskar v Laskar).
modelAnswer.application: Because Elif is Deniz's adult child, the presumption of advancement is in play on the father-to-child relationship and would presume a gift of Deniz's contribution absent contrary evidence. However, the purchase is for investment/letting purposes, not as Elif's home — the Laskar framing confirms the resulting trust analysis is the right lens, and the purpose of the transaction is itself strong evidence against a gift being intended, since gifting 70% of an investment property to a co-investor while retaining no formal interest would be an unusual arrangement absent explicit agreement. This evidence is capable of rebutting the presumption of advancement.
modelAnswer.conclusion: On these facts, the presumption of advancement is likely rebutted by the investment character of the purchase, and Deniz has a strong claim to a resulting trust reflecting his 70% contribution — though the presumption's existence means Elif's argument cannot simply be dismissed and turns on the strength of the rebutting evidence.

testPool.prompt: A man transfers a rental property into his same-sex civil partner's sole name for no consideration. Which presumption applies?
options: The presumption of advancement, on the same basis as husband-to-wife transfers, since civil partnership is treated analogously for this purpose
No presumption applies at all because the relationship is not marriage
A resulting trust is automatically excluded because the property was already income-producing
testPool.trapExplanation: Students sometimes assume the old husband-to-wife categories are frozen and inapplicable outside opposite-sex marriage. Courts have extended the presumption of advancement by analogy to civil partners on the same reasoning as spouses; the presumption is not simply unavailable because the couple is not married in the traditional sense.

testPool.prompt: How settled is it that Westdeutsche's intention-based account of resulting trusts, rather than the unjust enrichment account, is currently the law in England and Wales?
sliderLabels: Highly unsettled — courts freely apply unjust enrichment instead
Settled as current law, though academically contested
testPool.explanation: Westdeutsche is binding House of Lords authority and states the current law: resulting trusts respond to intention, not unjust enrichment. The unjust enrichment analysis remains an influential academic critique, but it has not displaced Westdeutsche as the operative legal test.

testPool.prompt: Under Westdeutsche, what triggers an automatic (as opposed to presumed) resulting trust?
options: A settlor's failure to dispose of the whole beneficial interest under an express trust
Evidence that the transferor did not intend a gift
A purchase made jointly with a family member

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The two most common mistakes here are treating 'resulting trust' as one undifferentiated doctrine rather than two distinct triggers, and assuming the presumption of advancement has been abolished by the Equality Act 2010. It hasn't — s 199 has never been commenced, and this remains live, examinable law.
